subject: english-language
title: The Department Store of Prestige
welcome_lead: Saks, Macy's, Klein's — three shops, three accents, one famous experiment. Enter Labov's New York.
meta_desc: Labov's 1966 department store study and the concept of overt prestige at A-Level English Language.
final_note: You have walked Labov's aisles and heard how class shapes the very r-sounds we make.

concepts.def: William Labov's 1966 study of rhotic /r/ in Saks, Macy's and S. Klein, showing higher-prestige stores produced more post-vocalic /r/.
Public, conscious value attached to standard or high-status forms; aspirational speakers shift toward them.
Hidden value of non-standard forms within in-groups, signalling solidarity (Trudgill 1974 Norwich).
Peter Trudgill (1974) found working-class men over-reported non-standard forms, demonstrating covert prestige.
A linguistic feature that varies across speakers (post-vocalic /r/, /h/-dropping, glottal stop).
Systematic patterning of variants by social class, age, gender or context.
A feature whose realisation correlates with social factors — Labov's central analytic unit.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Labov asked clerks for directions to the fourth floor, eliciting fourth and floor — two tokens of post-vocalic /r/. He then feigned mishearing to force a careful repetition.

Saks (high prestige) produced /r/ most, Klein's (low prestige) least, with Macy's between. Casual style showed less /r/ than emphatic repetition — speakers shifted toward the prestigious variant when monitoring speech.

Trudgill investigated -ing versus -in' in Norwich. Self-report data showed working-class men claimed to use the non-standard form more than they did.

The non-standard form carried covert prestige — masculinity, toughness, in-group loyalty.
Sociolinguistics treats variation as orderly, not chaotic. By correlating phonetic variants with class, age, gender and style, Labov turned dialect study into quantitative science.
